description_full: Oshkosh Corporation provides purpose-built vehicles and equipment worldwide. The company operates through three segments: Access, Vocational, and Transport segment. The Access segment designs and manufactures aerial work platform and telehandlers for use in construction, industrial, and maintenance applications; and towing and recovery equipment, which includes carriers, wreckers, and rotators, as well as provides financing and leasing solutions, including rental fleet loans, leases, and floor plan and retail financing. This segment also offers equipment installation and sale of chassis and service parts, as well as offers parts and accessories. The Transport segment engages in the manufacture and sale of heavy, medium, and light tactical wheeled vehicles and related services for defense; and hauling combat vehicles, missile systems, ammunition, fuel, and troops and cargos. The Vocational segment offers custom and commercial firefighting equipment, fire apparatus, and emergency vehicles, including pumpers, aerial platform, ladder and tiller trucks, and tankers; light, medium, and heavy-duty rescue vehicles; and wildland rough terrain response other emergency response vehicles. This segment also produces and sells aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicles; airport ground support equipment; baggage, airport facility and operations, and equipment-monitoring technology services; refuse and recycling collection vehicles and components; and IMT-branded field service vehicles and truck-mounted cranes, frontline communications-branded simulators, command vehicles and other communication vehicles, and front-discharge concrete mixer vehicles. The company sells its products through direct sales representatives, dealers, and distributors. The company was formerly known as Oshkosh Truck Corporation. Oshkosh Corporation was founded in 1915 and is headquartered in Oshkosh, Wisconsin.

financial_summary: Oshkosh Corporation (Holding Co is a mid-cap industrials business with a $8.8B market cap on $10.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 17% against a 10% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 17% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $618M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.21× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 8.0×.

Shareholder yield of 4.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 9% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 6% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 7% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 20% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 1.04, it moves roughly with the market.
About $77.7M trades a day, enough to build a position.

val: The stock trades 43% below its DCF fair value of $256, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 44%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $114 to $618 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 18.3 vs 23.1, EV/EBITDA 9.5 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 14.3 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 8% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 7.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 10.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 17 covering analysts target $159 on average, 10% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 9.6% by 7pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.45).
It runs a 17% gross margin and converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.21x.
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.7% of revenue on R&D and 0.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.5x net debt to EBITDA ($479.8M of cash against $1.1B of debt), with interest covered 8.0x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.3, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.0% over 3 years, 8.7% over 5 years and 5.5% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 16.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 23.5% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.03, a backlog worth 1.2x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 9%.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (1.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 14, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 4.6% a year to shareholders (3.2% in buybacks and 1.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 13 consecutive years, raising it 9.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 18,400 employees, each generates about $566K of revenue, 1.6x the Industrials median.
That works out to $34K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.9M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
